translationRepairs: Early in the Tongguang reign, Prince Wei Ji Ji served as director of the Xingsheng Palace while also holding the military commission of Zhen Prefecture, and Song went with him as adjutant.
Early in the Tongguang reign, Prince of Wei Jiji served as director of the Xingsheng Palace while also holding the military commission of Zhen Prefecture, and Song went with him as adjutant.
Chinese 魏王繼岌 is Prince of Wei, personal name Jiji (繼岌), not two given names Ji Ji.
At the beginning of the Tongguang era, Prince Wei Ji Ji was Director of the Xingsheng Palace and concurrently held the military commission of Zhen Prefecture; Song accompanied him as adjutant.

The judicial officer (tuiguan) Li Rao then handled correspondence, and Song, finding his drafts clumsy, quietly told the steward Lü Rou, "His Lordship is an imperial prince, the hope of the realm; whatever letters and memorials go out should at least be literate and apt.
推官 is a staff judicial officer, not investigating censor; 蕘 is Rao; 令公皇子 refers to the prince as imperial son.

When the imperial forces marched against Shu, Jiji was overall commander and Song served as his chief secretary.
Personal name 繼岌 should be romanized Jiji, not Ji Ji.

The future Jin founder was then deputy commander of the Six Armies; with Prince Qin Congrong plotting treason, he urgently sought a post away from court and dearly hoped for the northern command, yet the senior ministers, knowing he already held the armies, hesitated to broach the appointment.

秦王從榮 is Prince of Qin plus personal name Congrong, not a fused English "Prince Qin Congrong".
